correctness.rationale: In this all-shortest-paths convexity, the distance is ceil(|b−a|/2). An even gap forces a unique path of jumps by two; an odd gap allows every intermediate vertex and no overshoot, by the distance equality test. Applying this to the extreme vertices and to any vertex of opposite parity gives exactly the asserted concepts. Counting intervals and proper step-two progressions yields the stated cardinalities. For three ordered points only the endpoint-only trace can fail, and it works exactly when both gaps are odd. Four-point shattering would require consecutive gaps odd to isolate the first and third and the second and fourth; then the first and fourth cannot be isolated. Summing the possible first vertices by the two odd gaps gives the stated static coefficients. Induction on version-space size proves the online recurrence because every usable query makes both subspaces strictly smaller. An independent tuple-based calculation reproduced all orders through 20, checked feasibility through rank plus one at orders 1–12, and verified 32 leaves of a depth-five tree at n=10. The n=10 first-query branch pairs match the frozen list, all with minimum at most four, ruling out depth six. Restricting to intervals through a central vertex leaves independent ordered endpoint thresholds on either side, giving the asymptotic lower bound by balanced search; the cardinality upper bound matches up to a constant.
residual_risks: The exact online spectrum is established through n=20 only; the universal asymptotic result is up to an additive constant.

value.rationale: The cutoff is the first failure of a natural optimal-depth bound in a natural graph family, not merely an arbitrarily chosen run of a generic algorithm. At order ten the concept count permits depth six, but exact root-branch ranks show why no query can support it, while depth five is attainable. The consecutive exact orders on both sides distinguish a first failure from a permanent drop (the bound is attained again at eleven and twelve).
residual_risks: The scientific contribution is a finite boundary and initial spectrum; neither a general optimal query policy nor an exact formula for larger orders is shown.
